transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study has found that people who regularly practice mindfulness meditation have lower levels of stress and anxiety and better overall mental health, according to researchers at Harvard University. The study followed over 200 adults who had never meditated before and randomly assigned them to either an 8-week mindfulness meditation program or a control group. They found that the people who meditated showed a 30 percent reduction in stress and anxiety symptoms, and they also had lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol in their blood. Brain scans also showed changes in the areas of the brain associated with emotion regulation and self-awareness. Mindfulness meditation involves focusing your attention on the present moment—your breath, your body sensations, your thoughts—without judgment. Researchers say it's a simple, low-cost way to improve mental health, and it can be practiced by almost anyone, anywhere. They note that you don't need any special equipment or a lot of time—even just 10 to 15 minutes a day can make a difference.

2. What is mindfulness meditation?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The city of London has announced plans to create a new network of "quiet ways"—cycle routes on quieter side streets that are designed to make cycling feel safer and more comfortable for people who don't want to ride on busy main roads. The routes will be separated from car traffic where possible, and they will have special signage and slower speed limits to make them more bike-friendly. The goal is to encourage more people to cycle, especially women and older people who are often put off by busy roads and heavy traffic. The city says that increasing cycling will reduce traffic congestion, improve air quality, and make the city healthier and more livable. London already has a well-known bike share program and many bike lanes, but many people still don't feel safe cycling on busy streets. The new quiet ways are designed to connect residential areas with workplaces, shops, and public transport hubs, making it easier for people to use bikes for everyday trips. The first quiet ways opened last year and have already been popular with cyclists, so the city is now expanding the network to cover more areas.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Scientists have developed a new type of artificial intelligence that can diagnose certain eye diseases as accurately as expert doctors, according to a study published in *Nature Medicine*. The AI system was trained on thousands of eye scans to recognize signs of diabetic retinopathy, a common complication of diabetes that can cause blindness if not detected and treated early. In tests, the AI system was able to correctly identify the disease with more than 94 percent accuracy, which is comparable to the performance of experienced ophthalmologists. Researchers say this technology could be especially useful in areas where there are not enough eye doctors, or in rural and low-income regions where access to specialized medical care is limited. It could also help speed up diagnosis and treatment, potentially saving people's vision. The AI system is still being tested and refined, but researchers hope it could be used in clinical settings within the next few years. They emphasize that the technology is meant to help doctors, not replace them, by providing faster and more consistent screening.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Emily): Hey Jack, I heard you just got back from your trip to Scotland. How was it?
Man (Jack): It was amazing! Scotland is so beautiful—mountains, lakes, castles... I had the best time. I'm so glad I went.
Woman: I've always wanted to go to Scotland. What was the best part?

Man: Oh, that's hard to say. Edinburgh was great—such a beautiful city with the castle and all the old buildings. And the Highlands were absolutely stunning. We drove through the Highlands and stopped at all these little villages and lakes. The scenery was just incredible.
Woman: That sounds amazing. Did you see the Loch Ness Monster?
Man: Ha, no, unfortunately not. We did go to Loch Ness though. It's a beautiful lake, even if there's no monster.
Woman: What was the weather like? I've heard it rains a lot in Scotland.

Man: Oh, it definitely rained. A lot. We had a few sunny days, but most days it was cloudy or rainy. But honestly, the rain kind of added to the atmosphere. The Highlands look even more dramatic in the rain, you know? And we just brought good rain jackets and waterproof boots, so it was fine.
Woman: That's a good attitude. What about the food? I've heard Scottish food is... interesting.

Man: Ha, yeah, it's not all haggis and deep-fried Mars bars, though those do exist. But actually, the food was a lot better than I expected. We had some amazing seafood—fresh fish and shellfish from the coast. And there are lots of great restaurants in Edinburgh. I did try haggis, actually, and it was better than I thought it would be. Not something I'd eat every day, but it was worth trying.
Woman: Wow, you're braver than me. I don't think I could eat haggis.

Man: It's really not that bad! You should try it if you ever go. What else... oh, the whiskey! Scotland is famous for its whiskey, of course. We did a whiskey distillery tour and learned all about how it's made. That was really interesting.
Woman: That sounds cool. Did you bring any back?
Man: Of course! I bought a few bottles. Some for me, some for my dad.
Woman: Nice. How long were you there for?

Man: We were there for 10 days. We spent a few days in Edinburgh, then drove around the Highlands for a week. It was the perfect amount of time—long enough to see a lot, but not so long that we got tired.
Woman: That sounds perfect. I really want to go now. Do you have any tips for someone planning a trip?

Man: Oh, definitely. First, bring layers and good rain gear. The weather changes all the time. Second, rent a car if you can—public transport in the Highlands is pretty limited, and having a car gives you so much more freedom to explore. And third, don't try to do too much. There's so much to see, but it's better to take your time and really enjoy a few places than to rush around trying to see everything.
Woman: That's good advice. Thanks, Jack. Now I'm even more excited to go someday.
Man: You should definitely go! It's one of the most beautiful places I've ever been.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (David): Hey Sarah, I need your advice. I'm thinking about getting a dog, but I'm not sure if I'm ready for the responsibility. What do you think?
Woman (Sarah): Oh, that's a big decision! Dogs are amazing, but they are a lot of work. Why do you want a dog?

Man: Well, I've always loved dogs, and I've wanted one for years. But I was always too busy with school and work. Now I have a more stable job and a bigger apartment, so I think maybe I'm ready. And I feel like having a dog would get me outside more and make me more active.

Woman: That's true—dogs definitely keep you active. But you have to be prepared for the commitment. Dogs need to be walked every day, multiple times a day. They need attention, training, vet visits, food... it's a lot of time and money. And they can live 10 to 15 years, so it's a long-term commitment.
Man: Yeah, I know. That's why I'm hesitating. I work 9 to 5, so I'd be gone for about 8 hours a day. Is that too long to leave a dog alone?

Woman: Hmm, that's a good question. It depends on the dog. Puppies definitely can't be left alone that long—they need to go out more often and they get lonely. But adult dogs can usually handle 8 hours alone, as long as they get plenty of exercise before and after work. You could also hire a dog walker to come in the middle of the day, or take the dog to doggy daycare a few days a week.
Man: That's a good idea. What kind of dog do you think would be good for me? I live in an apartment, so probably not a huge dog.

Woman: Yeah, apartment living is better for smaller or medium-sized dogs, and breeds that are less energetic. But it also depends on how much exercise you can give them. If you're willing to take them for long walks and go to the dog park on weekends, you can have a more active dog even in an apartment. What kind of dogs do you like?
Man: I like all dogs, but I think I'd want something friendly and not too hyper. Maybe a rescue dog? I'd like to adopt instead of buying from a breeder.

Woman: That's great! There are so many dogs in shelters that need good homes. And shelter dogs come in all sizes and personalities. You should go to a shelter and meet some dogs—you'll know when you find the right one.
Man: Yeah, I think I'd like that. But I'm worried about getting a dog with behavior problems or something.

Woman: That's a valid concern, but most shelters evaluate the dogs' temperaments and can tell you about their personalities and any issues they might have. And a lot of behavior problems can be fixed with training and patience. You could also consider getting an older dog instead of a puppy—older dogs are often already house-trained and calmer, which might be better for someone who works full-time.
Man: That's a good point. Puppies are a lot of work, right?

Woman: Oh my goodness, puppies are so much work. They need constant attention, they chew everything, they have accidents in the house... it's like having a baby. If you work full-time, a puppy would be really hard. An adult dog would probably be a better fit for you.
Man: Yeah, that makes sense. What about costs? How much does having a dog cost, roughly?

Woman: It varies, but you should expect to spend at least a few hundred dollars a month on food, vet bills, toys, and other supplies. And then there are unexpected vet bills if the dog gets sick or injured, which can be really expensive. You should make sure you can afford it before you get a dog.
Man: Hmm, okay. That's more than I thought. But I think I can handle it.
Woman: Also, think about your lifestyle. Do you travel a lot? If you do, you'll need to find someone to take care of the dog when you're gone, which adds to the cost.
Man: I travel occasionally, but not that often. I could probably ask my sister to watch the dog, or board it at a kennel.
Woman: That's good. Well, it sounds like you've thought about this a lot. I think you'd be a great dog owner. You just have to make sure you're really ready for the commitment.
Man: Yeah, I know. Thanks for all the advice, Sarah. You've given me a lot to think about.
Woman: No problem! Let me know if you decide to get one—I'd love to meet your new dog.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The history of the bicycle is a story of innovation and evolution that spans over 200 years. From the earliest wooden walking machines to the modern high-tech bikes we have today, bicycles have changed dramatically, but their basic purpose—providing simple, efficient human-powered transportation—has remained the same.

The earliest ancestor of the bicycle was the "draisine," invented by Karl von Drais in Germany in 1817. It was a wooden frame with two wheels, but it had no pedals—you pushed it along with your feet, like a scooter. It was popular for a while, but it was uncomfortable and not very practical.

In the 1860s, the first real bicycle with pedals was invented in France. These early bikes, called "velocipedes," had pedals attached directly to the front wheel. They were nicknamed "boneshakers" because they were so uncomfortable to ride on cobblestone streets.

Then, in the 1870s and 1880s, the "penny-farthing" or "high-wheel" bicycle became popular. These bikes had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel, and you sat way up high. They were faster than previous bikes, but they were also very dangerous—if you hit a bump, you could go flying over the handlebars.

The modern bicycle as we know it today appeared in the 1880s with the invention of the "safety bicycle," which had two wheels of the same size and a chain drive to power the rear wheel. This design was much safer and more practical, and it quickly replaced the penny-farthing. The safety bicycle is basically the same design we use today.

Bicycles became extremely popular in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. They were affordable, efficient transportation, and they gave people—especially women—more freedom and mobility. The bicycle craze of the 1890s even had social and cultural effects, changing fashion, promoting women's rights, and creating new forms of recreation.

Today, bicycles are more popular than ever. They're used for transportation, recreation, sport, and exercise. In many cities around the world, cycling is becoming an increasingly important part of the transportation system, as people look for alternatives to cars that are cheaper, healthier, and better for the environment.

Modern bicycles are made with advanced materials like carbon fiber and aluminum, and they come in all kinds of specialized designs—road bikes, mountain bikes, hybrid bikes, electric bikes, and more. But the basic principle is still the same as it was 200 years ago: human power, two wheels, and the simple joy of riding.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Animal communication is a fascinating field of study that explores how animals share information with each other. While animals don't have language in the same way humans do, they use a wide variety of methods to communicate—sounds, body language, scents, and even electrical signals. Understanding how animals communicate gives us insight into their social lives, intelligence, and emotions.

One of the most well-known examples of animal communication is the honeybee's "waggle dance." When a honeybee finds a good source of food, it returns to the hive and performs a special dance that tells the other bees exactly where the food is located. The direction and length of the dance convey information about the direction and distance of the food source. This is an incredibly sophisticated form of communication that allows bees to share detailed information with each other.

Many animals use vocalizations to communicate. Birds sing to mark their territory and attract mates. Wolves howl to communicate with other members of their pack over long distances. Elephants use low-frequency rumbles that can travel for miles through the ground to communicate with other elephants far away. Dolphins and whales use complex songs and clicks to communicate with each other underwater.

Body language is another important form of animal communication. Dogs, for example, use their tails, ears, and body posture to communicate their mood and intentions. A wagging tail usually means a dog is happy or excited, while flattened ears and a lowered body mean the dog is scared or submissive. Primates like chimpanzees and gorillas use a wide range of facial expressions and gestures to communicate with each other, much like humans do.

Many animals also use chemical communication—scents and pheromones—to mark territory, attract mates, and signal alarm. Ants leave chemical trails that other ants follow to find food. Cats rub their faces on objects to leave their scent and mark their territory.

While animal communication is complex and sophisticated, it's different from human language in important ways. Human language is symbolic, grammatical, and can be used to create an infinite number of new sentences and ideas. Animal communication is usually more limited and tied to specific situations—food, danger, mating, territory. But scientists are still learning about the full extent of animal communication, and new discoveries are being made all the time.
Studying animal communication not only helps us understand animals better—it also gives us insight into the evolution of language and what makes human language unique.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Climate change is one of the most pressing challenges facing the world today. The Earth's climate is changing at an unprecedented rate, with global temperatures rising, ice caps melting, sea levels rising, and extreme weather events becoming more frequent and more intense. The overwhelming consensus among scientists is that this climate change is primarily caused by human activities, especially the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil, and natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.

Greenhouse gases work like a blanket around the Earth, trapping heat from the sun and keeping the planet warm enough for life to exist. This is the natural greenhouse effect, and without it, the Earth would be too cold to live on. But since the Industrial Revolution, humans have been releasing huge amounts of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels for energy, transportation, and industry, and by cutting down forests that would otherwise absorb carbon dioxide. This enhanced greenhouse effect is causing the planet to warm up faster than it ever has naturally.

The consequences of climate change are already being felt around the world. Global average temperatures have risen by about 1 degree Celsius since pre-industrial times. Glaciers and ice sheets are melting, causing sea levels to rise, which threatens coastal cities and communities with flooding and erosion. Extreme weather events like heatwaves, hurricanes, droughts, and wildfires are becoming more frequent and more severe. Climate change also affects agriculture, water supplies, ecosystems, and human health.

The good news is that we know what we need to do to address climate change. We need to dramatically reduce our greenhouse gas emissions by transitioning from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources like solar, wind, and hydro power. We need to make our buildings, transportation, and industries more energy efficient. We need to protect and restore forests and other natural ecosystems that absorb carbon dioxide. And we need to adapt to the changes that are already happening and can't be avoided.

Addressing climate change will require action at all levels—from individuals to governments to businesses. Individuals can reduce their carbon footprint by driving less, using energy more efficiently, eating less meat, and reducing waste. Governments can create policies and regulations to encourage clean energy, reduce emissions, and invest in climate solutions. Businesses can innovate and develop new technologies and practices that are more sustainable.

While climate change is a huge and daunting challenge, it's not impossible to solve. With the right policies, technologies, and collective action, we can still avoid the worst impacts of climate change and build a more sustainable future. But we need to act now—every year we wait makes the problem worse and harder to fix.
